---
title: "Replicating Hajian-Forooshani & Chase (2026)"
---

Hajian-Forooshani & Chase (2026) asked why disturbance increases beta diversity in some
metacommunities and decreases it in others. They added a single pulse disturbance to the model
of Thompson et al. (2020): for 100 time steps, the environment of a random set of patches falls
below the optima of all species, and then returns to its previous value. Disturbance thus acts
on growth rates through the niche, not by removing individuals. Their central result is that
dispersal sets the direction of the change in beta diversity. In dispersal-limited
metacommunities, disturbed patches are slow to be recolonised, local richness falls more than
regional richness, and beta diversity increases (differentiation). With a dispersal surplus,
local richness recovers fast while species are lost from the whole landscape, and beta
diversity decreases (homogenisation). At intermediate dispersal, the direction depends on the
extent of the disturbance and on niche breadth. Because their model is that of Thompson et al.
(2020), it is a special case of `simulate_metacommunity()`, and the replication only needed a
way to write the pulse, `env_pulse()`. Like the [replication of Urban & De Meester
(2009)](replication-urban.html), this article is part of the [nesting map](nesting-map.html) of
the package.

## Translation of the model

The script `data-raw/replication_hajian2026.R` follows the code archived with the article
(Figshare, doi:10.6084/m9.figshare.30620603.v1), which fills in parameters that the text does
not give:

* 100 patches on a 10 × 10 grid wrapped as a torus, with the dispersal kernel
  \(\exp(-0.1\,d)\), that is `landscape_grid(side = 10, disp_scale = 10, torus = TRUE)`;
* 30 species with optima drawn from U(0.5, 1), \(r_{max} = 5\) and a niche breadth \(n\) shared
  by all species. Their code computes growth as \(r_{max}\exp(-((z - e)/(2n))^2)\), so
  \(\sigma = \sqrt{2}\,n\) in `growth_rates()`, which uses \(\exp(-(z - e)^2/(2\sigma^2))\);
* intraspecific competition \(0.5 \times 0.05\) and interspecific coefficients drawn from
  U(0, 1) × 0.05, so that the mean interspecific coefficient equals the intraspecific one; the
  matrix is asymmetric and was passed as is, not built with `competition_matrix()`;
* the environment of each patch drawn from U(0.5, 1), without spatial autocorrelation;
* at step 500, a random 1 or 5% to 100% of patches set to an environment of 0.1 for steps 500
  to 600, `env_pulse(env, 1000, sites, start = 500, duration = 101, value = 0.1)`;
* Poisson(1) individuals of every species in every patch at the start and no later seeding
  (`seed_steps = numeric(0)`, `seed_mean = 1`), 1000 steps, and no extirpation, so the
  landscape is closed and regional richness can only fall;
* local richness \(\alpha\) is the mean richness of all patches, disturbed or not, and regional
  richness \(\gamma\) that of the landscape; changes are log ratios relative to step 499, and
  \(\Delta\beta = \Delta\gamma - \Delta\alpha\), the log ratio of Whittaker's beta, as in the
  script of their Fig. 2.

We ran 100 replicates for each combination of niche breadth (0.2, 0.25, 0.3, 0.4), dispersal
(\(10^{-5}\), \(10^{-4}\), \(10^{-3}\)) and extent (21 values), with a new landscape, species
pool and competition matrix in each replicate.

### Differences from their implementation

* **Redistribution of emigrants.** Their code pools all emigrants of a species and sends each
  one to a patch with probability proportional to the expected inflow from the other patches,
  so an emigrant can land back in its own patch. We used `immigration = "multinomial"`, which
  distributes the emigrants of each patch among the other patches by the kernel. Both conserve
  individuals. The kernel is nearly flat (two patches of the grid are at most 7.1 cells apart,
  and \(\exp(-0.71) = 0.49\)), so the difference should be small.
* **Article and code.** The text calls \(n\) the standard deviation of the Gaussian niche and
  gives the disturbed environment only as below 0.5; the code uses \(((z - e)/(2n))^2\), a
  Gaussian with standard deviation \(\sqrt{2}\,n\), and an environment of 0.1. We followed the
  code. With it, species with optima near 0.5 keep positive growth in disturbed patches at every
  niche breadth studied: with \(n = 0.2\), a species with optimum 0.5 grows at
  \(r = 5e^{-1} = 1.8\) at an environment of 0.1. The pulse therefore filters species by their
  optima, the "disturbance tolerant" species of the article, rather than emptying the disturbed
  patches.
* **Replicates.** The legends of their figures give 100 replicates; the archived code runs 50.

## Dispersal sets the direction of the change in beta diversity

The replication reproduces their Fig. 2 qualitatively (figure below, \(n = 0.25\), 100 steps
after the end of the pulse). In dispersal-limited metacommunities (\(d = 10^{-5}\)), local
richness fell more than regional richness at every extent, and beta diversity increased, from
\(\Delta\beta = 0.007\) with one disturbed patch to 0.60 with 80% of the landscape disturbed.
With a dispersal surplus (\(d = 10^{-3}\)), local richness recovered almost completely while
regional richness kept falling, and beta diversity decreased at every extent, from \(-0.07\) to
\(-0.88\) with the whole landscape disturbed. At intermediate dispersal (\(d = 10^{-4}\)), the
direction depended on the extent, as in the article: beta diversity decreased slightly when
1–10% of the landscape was disturbed (\(-0.04\) to \(-0.01\)), did not change at 15–20%,
increased from 25% to 95% (up to 0.21 at 75%), and
decreased again when the whole landscape was disturbed (\(-0.32\)). We cannot compare the
magnitudes with theirs from the figures alone; their simulated data are archived with the
code (a 106 MB file) and would allow a quantitative comparison.

![Changes in local (\(\Delta\alpha\)) and regional (\(\Delta\gamma\)) richness and in beta diversity (\(\Delta\beta\)) between step 499 and step 700, against the percentage of the landscape disturbed, for niche breadth \(n = 0.25\). Means and 95% confidence intervals of 100 replicates. Dashed lines: the same changes in metacommunities without disturbance. Notice that with intermediate and high dispersal the undisturbed metacommunities also homogenise.](hajian_fig2.png)

## Recovery and niche breadth

Over the recovery phase (their Fig. 3), the replication also follows the article. Without
recolonisation, dispersal-limited metacommunities kept the increase in beta diversity until
step 1000. With a dispersal surplus, local richness regained most of its loss within 50 steps
of the end of the pulse (with \(n = 0.25\) and half of the landscape disturbed, from
\(\Delta\alpha = -0.32\) at step 601 to \(-0.09\) at step 650), whereas regional richness kept
falling, so beta diversity kept decreasing. At intermediate dispersal, niche breadth changed the outcome: at step 700, with
half of the landscape disturbed, beta diversity increased with narrow niches (\(n = 0.2\),
\(\Delta\beta = 0.18\)), less with intermediate ones (0.07 for \(n = 0.3\)), and not with broad
ones (\(-0.01\) for \(n = 0.4\)). Losses with narrow niches grew nonlinearly with the extent,
and with broad niches nearly linearly. With narrow niches and the whole landscape disturbed,
the whole metacommunity went extinct in 2 of 100 replicates with \(d = 10^{-5}\) and 6 with
\(d = 10^{-3}\); these were left out of the means, as in their script of Fig. 3. We did not
replicate their Fig. 4, which separates regional extinctions during and after the pulse.

![Changes in local (solid) and regional (dashed) richness from step 499 to steps 601–1000 (lighter colours: later steps), against the percentage of the landscape disturbed, for three niche breadths (rows) and three dispersal rates (columns). Means of 100 replicates.](hajian_fig3.png)

## Not all of the homogenisation is caused by the disturbance

The smallest extent in the article is one patch of 100, so it has no control without
disturbance. We added one (100 replicates per setting, with seeds of their own), and it shows
that the metacommunities are not at equilibrium at step 499 when dispersal is intermediate or
high. Without any disturbance, regional richness kept falling through competitive exclusion
while local richness did not, so that beta diversity decreased by itself: with \(n = 0.25\),
\(\Delta\beta = -0.05\) at step 700 and \(-0.12\) at step 1000 with \(d = 10^{-4}\), and
\(-0.07\) and \(-0.14\) with \(d = 10^{-3}\). With dispersal limitation it did not change
(\(|\Delta\beta| < 0.005\)).

The effect of the disturbance is the difference from the control, as in a
before-after-control-impact design. On that scale, at step 700 and with \(n = 0.25\):

* with dispersal limitation, nothing changes, since the control is flat: the disturbance
  increases beta diversity at every extent, by up to 0.60;
* at intermediate dispersal, the disturbance increases beta diversity at every extent from one
  patch to 95% of the landscape (by 0.009 to 0.26), and decreases it only when the whole
  landscape is disturbed (\(-0.27\)). The homogenisation at small extents is background, so the
  dependence of the direction on the extent reduces to a reversal at complete disturbance;
* with a dispersal surplus, the disturbance adds less than 0.025 to the background decline
  until a quarter of the landscape is disturbed, about 0.05 at half, and 0.81 when all of it is.

The shift towards homogenisation over the recovery phase at intermediate dispersal (their
Fig. 3b) also follows the background decline: by step 1000, the control alone has
\(\Delta\beta = -0.12\). A longer burn-in before the pulse, or the difference from paired
undisturbed runs, would separate the two.

In short, comdynamite reproduces the patterns of Hajian-Forooshani & Chase (2026) with
`env_pulse()` and no change to its engine. The paired control shows that part of the
homogenisation they report at intermediate and high dispersal comes from the transient
dynamics of the metacommunity rather than from the disturbance, while the differentiation
under dispersal limitation and the homogenisation after extensive disturbance with a dispersal
surplus are effects of the disturbance itself. We did not check whether a longer burn-in
removes the background decline in their own simulations; their archived data would show it.

Viana, D. S., & Chase, J. M. (2020). A process-based metacommunity framework linking local and
regional scale community ecology. *Ecology Letters*, 23, 1314–1329.
